candidate_analysis.explanation: The Random Forest assigns this binary to the malware class with probability 1.0000, and all 20 top n-grams push the prediction toward cryptojacking. The evidence itself is weak and non-specific, though. SHAP contributions are small and evenly spread, from +0.013321 (ADD POP) down to +0.006492 (XOR CALL), so no single feature dominates. Eight of the 20 n-grams have a relative frequency of 0.000000 (ADD POP, CMOVZ MOV, CALL ADD, LEA CALL, XOR XOR, TEST JS, XOR CALL). Their contribution comes from the model treating their absence as a malware signal, not from any observed code pattern. The n-grams that are present occur at low frequency (about 0.002 to 0.040). Most are generic stack and arithmetic sequences (POP SUB, CALL PUSH, ADD PUSH, SUB PUSH, POP CALL, POP MOV, POP PUSH, POP ADD, INC PUSH, ADD ADD) that reflect function prologues, epilogues and call setup. A few carry-flag sequences (MOV ADC at 0.031621, ADC SUB, XOR ADC) are loosely consistent with multi-word arithmetic, which cryptographic or hashing code can use. They are also common in ordinary compiled code, and the evidence lists no functions, so they cannot be tied to a mining routine. The evidence has no rotate/shift-heavy or vectorized sequences and no function-level context that would tie the patterns to mining. The model's classification is a strong statistical signal, but the listed n-grams do not on their own show cryptojacking behavior, so the result is inconclusive.
